name: Trauma Test
tagline: Check how a very stressful experience may still be affecting you.
intro: Think of one very stressful experience that still affects you and keep it in mind while answering. For each problem, the question is: In the past month, how much were you bothered by… This screener includes the PCL-5, a widely used checklist for post-traumatic stress, plus extra questions about intrusive memories, avoidance, mood and feeling on edge. It takes about five minutes and is not a diagnosis.
seoTitle: Trauma Test – Free PCL-5 based PTSD screener
seoDescription: Does a stressful experience still affect you? Take this 5-minute trauma screener with the PCL-5 and get a personal report on four symptom areas.
items: Repeated, disturbing, and unwanted memories of the stressful experience
Repeated, disturbing dreams of the stressful experience
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again (as if you were actually back there reliving it)
Feeling very upset when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience (for example, heart pounding, trouble breathing, sweating)
Avoiding memories, thoughts, or feelings related to the stressful experience
Avoiding external reminders of the stressful experience (for example, people, places, conversations, activities, objects, or situations)
Trouble remembering important parts of the stressful experience

Having strong negative beliefs about yourself, other people, or the world (for example, having thoughts such as: I am bad, there is something seriously wrong with me, no one can be trusted, the world is completely dangerous)
Blaming yourself or someone else for the stressful experience or what happened after it
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Feeling distant or cut off from other people

Losing track of the present because a memory took over
Feeling unsafe, even in familiar places
Feeling permanently changed for the worse
Staying away from people connected to what happened
Sudden flashes of fear without knowing why
Struggling to relax, even when nothing is wrong
Feeling guilty that others were affected more than you
Having a racing heart for no obvious reason
Feeling the same emotions as during the experience, out of nowhere
Using alcohol, drugs or food to avoid feelings about it
Losing trust in people you used to trust
Replaying the experience over and over in your mind
Feeling sad or tearful for much of the day
Feeling on edge around strangers
Cancelling plans that could bring up memories
Needing a long time to calm down after a memory comes up
Losing patience with people you care about
Avoiding certain smells, sounds or music
Feeling like a different person since it happened
Certain sounds or smells bringing the experience back instantly
Feeling hopeless about things getting better
Changing the subject when someone brings it up
Waking up at the slightest sound
Freezing when something reminds you of the experience
Feeling lonely, even with people who care about you
Avoiding being alone with your thoughts
Sitting with your back to the wall to watch people
Crying unexpectedly when something brings back the memory
Feeling bitter about what happened
Not allowing yourself to feel sad or scared about it
Feeling restless and unable to sit still
Losing your sense of meaning or faith
Staying at home to avoid possible reminders
Memories of the experience interrupting your work or conversations
Grinding your teeth or clenching your jaw
Seeing the faces or places involved when you close your eyes
Feeling disconnected from your own body or surroundings
Feeling exhausted from always being on alert
Avoiding situations that feel similar to the experience
Feeling unworthy since the experience
Overreacting to things that feel threatening
Not asking for help because it means facing what happened
Feeling pain or tension in your body linked to the memory
Doubting your own judgement since it happened
Finding it hard to focus because you are watching your surroundings
Deleting photos or messages linked to the experience
Memories of what happened coming back in vivid detail
Needing to be in control of every situation
Putting off sleep because of what might come up
Being caught off guard by reminders in films, news or social media
Feeling a sense of dread for most of the day
Feeling panic as a date or anniversary approaches
Having headaches or stomach aches from stress
Downplaying what happened, to yourself or to others

intrusions.name: Intrusive memories
intrusions.short: How much unwanted memories, dreams or reliving of the experience bother you.
intrusions.low: Your answers suggest that memories of the stressful experience do not intrude much on your daily life at the moment. You may still think about it at times, which is natural, but it does not seem to overwhelm you. Keep looking after yourself with rest, connection and activities that help you feel grounded, and notice if this changes, for example around anniversaries.
intrusions.mid: Your answers suggest that memories, dreams or reminders of the experience bother you to a moderate degree. This is a common response after something very stressful, and for many people it eases with time and support. Grounding techniques, such as naming things you can see and hear around you, can help when a memory takes over. Talking with someone you trust may also lighten the load.
intrusions.high: Your answers suggest that unwanted memories, nightmares or the feeling of reliving the experience bother you a lot. This can be frightening and exhausting, and it is a recognised response to trauma, not a sign of weakness. Effective trauma-focused therapies exist, so please consider talking to a doctor or a qualified mental health professional. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away. Grounding exercises can offer some relief in the meantime.

avoidance.name: Avoidance
avoidance.short: How much you avoid thoughts, feelings, people or places linked to the experience.
avoidance.low: Your answers suggest that you are not strongly avoiding thoughts, feelings or situations connected to the experience. That openness usually helps people process what happened over time. It is still fine to choose when and with whom you talk about it. Keep doing the things that matter to you and that help you feel safe and supported. If avoidance increases during stressful periods, gently notice it without judging yourself.
avoidance.mid: Your answers suggest that you avoid some reminders, conversations or feelings linked to the experience. Avoidance brings short-term relief, but over time it can keep fear alive and make your world smaller. Try gently approaching situations that feel safe but uncomfortable, at your own pace, and share what you are going through with someone you trust. Small, manageable steps are enough; there is no need to rush.
avoidance.high: Your answers suggest that you go to great lengths to avoid anything that reminds you of the experience, including your own thoughts and feelings. This is understandable, but strong avoidance can keep distress in place and limit your life. Trauma-focused therapy can help you face memories safely and at your own pace, so please consider talking to a qualified mental health professional. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

negative_mood.name: Negative thoughts and mood
negative_mood.short: How much the experience has changed your mood, beliefs and sense of connection.
negative_mood.low: Your answers suggest that the experience has not strongly changed how you see yourself, others or the world, and that you still feel connected to people and to positive emotions. This is a sign of resilience. Keep nurturing the relationships and activities that give you meaning, and allow yourself space for feelings whenever they come up. If difficult thoughts appear later, talking them through early can prevent them from growing.
negative_mood.mid: Your answers suggest that the experience has affected your mood or beliefs to some degree. You may feel more guilt, mistrust, sadness or distance from others than before. These reactions are common and understandable. Try to stay in contact with people who support you, and gently question harsh thoughts about yourself. Writing about your feelings can also help to process them.
negative_mood.high: Your answers suggest that the experience has deeply affected your mood and beliefs, with strong feelings such as guilt, shame, numbness or disconnection from others. These changes can make life feel heavy and lonely, and they are a recognised part of post-traumatic stress. Please consider talking to a doctor or a qualified mental health professional, as effective help exists. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

hyperarousal.name: Feeling on edge
hyperarousal.short: How alert, tense, irritable or easily startled you have felt.
hyperarousal.low: Your answers suggest that you are not constantly on edge. You seem able to relax, sleep reasonably well and feel safe in everyday situations. This is a good foundation for recovery and wellbeing. Keep supporting your nervous system with regular exercise, sleep and time spent in calm, safe places with people you trust. If tension rises during busy or stressful weeks, short relaxation moments can help you reset.
hyperarousal.mid: Your answers suggest that you often feel tense, alert or irritable, and that relaxing or sleeping may be harder than before. Your body may still be in protection mode after the experience. Breathing exercises, regular movement and limiting caffeine can calm your nervous system. Try to create predictable, safe routines, especially around bedtime. If tension keeps building despite these steps, consider discussing it with your doctor.
hyperarousal.high: Your answers suggest that you feel on guard, tense, jumpy or irritable much of the time, and that sleep and concentration may be strongly affected. Your body seems to be stuck in alarm mode, which is exhausting. This is a recognised response to trauma and can improve with the right treatment. Please consider talking to a doctor or a qualified mental health professional. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

summary: This report combines your PCL-5 score, a widely used screening measure for post-traumatic stress, with four symptom areas. Higher scores mean you were bothered more over the past month. It is not a diagnosis; if your scores are raised, please talk to a doctor or qualified professional. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

instrument.name: PCL-5 score
instrument.description: The PCL-5 is a public-domain checklist for symptoms of post-traumatic stress, developed by the U.S. National Center for PTSD. A score of about 31–33 or higher suggests that a professional assessment may be helpful; it is a screening tool, not a diagnosis.
